title: MDCAT Test Day: What to Bring and What to Expect
excerpt: A practical rundown of what MDCAT test day actually looks like — documents to bring, arrival timing, and what the paper-based format means for how you should prepare.

content.text: Your admit card is the final word — read it carefully

Before anything else: your admit card (roll number slip) is the single most important document for test day, and it's also where PMDC will list the exact requirements for your specific test center and session. Details like arrival time and any center-specific instructions can be specified there, so read it carefully once it's issued rather than relying only on general guidance — including this post.

Download and print your admit card as soon as it's available, and read the instruction booklet that comes with it in full. Test-day rules are set by PMDC and communicated through official channels — treat your admit card as the authoritative source over anything you've read elsewhere, including here.
Based on PMDC's own published requirements for MDCAT candidates, you should expect to need:

items: Your printed admit card / roll number slip
Your original CNIC, B-Form, or passport (whichever you used to register) — a photocopy is generally not accepted as a substitute for the original
Your original Matriculation certificate, particularly if it carries your photograph
If you're under 18, a Juvenile Registration Certificate (JRC) issued by NADRA — this is a newly introduced requirement for the current cycle, separate from and in addition to your CNIC or B-Form

content.text: If you've lost your CNIC or B-Form, a NADRA token slip showing you've applied for a replacement is generally accepted as proof — but confirm this is still valid for your specific test date, since document policies can be updated.
Bring more than one copy of any document you're unsure about, and don't wait until the morning of the test to realize a document has expired or gone missing.
Arrive earlier than you think you need to

Test centers typically expect candidates to arrive well before the actual start time, since checking identification and seating a large number of candidates takes time — and entry is generally cut off at a fixed point regardless of when the test itself begins. Being late by even a few minutes past the entry cutoff can mean you're not allowed in at all, independent of what caused the delay.
Plan your route to the test center in advance, account for traffic and the unpredictability of exam-day mornings, and aim to arrive with a comfortable buffer rather than cutting it close.
What the paper-based format means for you

MDCAT is currently conducted as a paper-based test using an OMR (bubble) answer sheet, not a computer-based format. This has a few practical implications worth preparing for specifically, not just knowing about:

items: You'll be marking answers by filling in bubbles on a separate answer sheet, which is a different physical skill than clicking an option on a screen — practicing with real OMR sheets during your mock tests, not just solving MCQs in a notebook or app, builds the muscle memory for this
Bring two blue or black ballpoint pens specifically — pencils, gel pens, and markers are typically not permitted for filling the OMR sheet, so don't rely on a pencil as a backup here
Bring a clean clipboard to write on, since test centers commonly require this and rarely provide one

Since it's paper-based, there's no built-in timer visible to you the way some computer-based tests provide — bring a way to track time that's actually permitted at your test center, and confirm what that is in advance, since electronic devices including smartwatches are typically restricted in test halls

content.text: MDCAT questions span a mix of difficulty levels rather than being uniformly hard or easy — PMDC has described the paper as weighted toward a moderate difficulty band, with smaller portions at the easier and harder ends. Practically, this means you shouldn't expect every question to be a struggle, but you also shouldn't expect to breeze through the whole paper — pacing yourself so you don't burn excessive time on the harder minority of questions, at the expense of moderate ones you could answer quickly, matters more than trying to solve every question perfectly in order.

items: Original CNIC / B-Form / passport (whichever matches your registration)
Two blue or black ballpoint pens — not pencils or gel pens
A clear plan for arrival time that builds in extra buffer

content.text: Most MDCAT test-day stress is avoidable stress — it comes from uncertainty about documents, timing, or format, not from the exam content itself. Read your admit card and instruction booklet thoroughly as soon as they're available, prepare your documents well ahead of time, practice with real OMR sheets so the format itself isn't a surprise, and build in more buffer time than you think you need for arrival. The content is what your months of prep were for; the logistics are what a bit of advance planning takes care of entirely.

items.question: What documents do I need to bring to MDCAT?
items.answer: Your printed admit card, original CNIC/B-Form/passport, your original Matriculation certificate, and — if you're under 18 — a Juvenile Registration Certificate (JRC) from NADRA, a newly introduced requirement in addition to your CNIC or B-Form.

items.question: Can I use a pencil to fill the MDCAT OMR sheet?
items.answer: No — MDCAT typically requires two blue or black ballpoint pens for the OMR sheet, with pencils, gel pens, and markers not permitted. Don't rely on a pencil as a backup.

items.question: Is MDCAT computer-based or paper-based?
items.answer: MDCAT is currently a paper-based test using an OMR (bubble) answer sheet, not a computer-based format. Practicing with real OMR sheets during mock tests, not just solving MCQs digitally, is worth doing specifically for this reason.

items.question: What happens if I lose my CNIC or B-Form before test day?
items.answer: A NADRA token slip showing you've applied for a replacement is generally accepted as proof, but confirm this is still valid for your specific test date since document policies can change.

items.question: Do I need to bring my own clipboard to MDCAT?
items.answer: Yes — a clean clipboard is a standard requirement at MDCAT test centers, which typically don't provide one, so bring your own.
